PROP
43
LIMITS VOTERS’ ABILITY TO RAISE REVENUES FOR LOCAL GOVERNMENT SERVICES. LEGISLATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by the Legislature
Limits voters’ ability to pass voter-proposed local special taxes by increasing percentage of votes needed to approve such ballot measures from a majority (over 50%) to two-thirds, beginning January 1, 2027. Fiscal Impact: Possibility that local government tax revenues will not go up as much in the future due to a higher vote threshold for certain taxes. Supporters: California Taxpayers Association; Family Business Association of California; California Hispanic Chambers of Commerce Opponents: California Professional Firefighters; California Federation of Teachers; Nurse Alliance of SEIU CA.
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: Certain local government taxes would require two-thirds approval by voters.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: Certain local government taxes could continue to be approved by voters with a majority vote.
ARGUMENTS
PRO
Prop. 43 protects taxpayers by restoring Proposition 13’s two-thirds vote requirement to pass local special taxes, including sales taxes, real estate taxes and utility taxes. Courts have allowed special interests to pass earmarked tax increases with fewer votes. Prop. 43 closes this loophole, protecting taxpayers, homeowners and renters. Vote yes.
CON
PROPOSITION 43 LIMITS VOTERS’ ABILITY TO FUND ESSENTIAL LOCAL SERVICES including fire protection, 911 response, schools, roads, hospitals and affordable housing. It doesn’t cut your taxes and lets just 33.4% of voters veto what nearly 67% want. Protect your vote and majority rule. Vote NO on Proposition 43.

# Proposition 43
Limits Voters’ Ability to Raise Revenues for Local Government Services.
Legislative Constitutional Amendment.
## Analysis of Measure
### Background
***Vote Thresholds for Local Taxes.*** The State Constitution allows local governments to increase taxes with local voter approval.
Tax increases can be put on a ballot by voters or a local governing board (such as a city council or board of supervisors).
Increases in some types of local taxes require a two-thirds vote to approve them, while other types of taxes require a majority (more than half) vote to approve them.
Some local tax increases are approved permanently, while others are approved for a limited period of time.
Before those taxes expire, voters can be asked whether to extend them.
### Proposal
***Requires Certain Local Taxes Receive Two-Thirds Approval by Voters.*** Under current law, local taxes that are used for a specific purpose require a two-thirds vote to be approved.
These are called special taxes.
However, recent court decisions have allowed special taxes that are *proposed by voters* to be approved with a majority vote.
Under Proposition 43, beginning on January 1, 2027, any new, increased, or extended local special taxes proposed by voters would require a two-thirds vote.

## Analysis of Measure
### Background
***Vote Thresholds for Local Taxes.*** The State Constitution allows local governments to increase taxes with local voter approval.
Tax increases can be put on a ballot by voters or a local governing board (such as a city council or board of supervisors).
Increases in some types of local taxes require a two-thirds vote to approve them, while other types of taxes require a majority (more than half) vote to approve them.
Some local tax increases are approved permanently, while others are approved for a limited period of time.
Before those taxes expire, voters can be asked whether to extend them.
### Proposal
***Requires Certain Local Taxes Receive Two-Thirds Approval by Voters.*** Under current law, local taxes that are used for a specific purpose require a two-thirds vote to be approved.
These are called special taxes.
However, recent court decisions have allowed special taxes that are *proposed by voters* to be approved with a majority vote.
Under Proposition 43, beginning on January 1, 2027, any new, increased, or extended local special taxes proposed by voters would require a two-thirds vote.

PROP
43
LIMITS VOTERS’ ABILITY TO RAISE REVENUES FOR LOCAL GOVERNMENT SERVICES. LEGISLATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by the Legislature
Limits voters’ ability to pass voter-proposed local special taxes by increasing percentage of votes needed to approve such ballot measures from a majority (over 50%) to two-thirds, beginning January 1, 2027. Fiscal Impact: Possibility that local government tax revenues will not go up as much in the future due to a higher vote threshold for certain taxes. Supporters: California Taxpayers Association; Family Business Association of California; California Hispanic Chambers of Commerce Opponents: California Professional Firefighters; California Federation of Teachers; Nurse Alliance of SEIU CA.
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: Certain local government taxes would require two-thirds approval by voters.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: Certain local government taxes could continue to be approved by voters with a majority vote.
ARGUMENTS
PRO
Prop. 43 protects taxpayers by restoring Proposition 13’s two-thirds vote requirement to pass local special taxes, including sales taxes, real estate taxes and utility taxes. Courts have allowed special interests to pass earmarked tax increases with fewer votes. Prop. 43 closes this loophole, protecting taxpayers, homeowners and renters. Vote yes.
CON
PROPOSITION 43 LIMITS VOTERS’ ABILITY TO FUND ESSENTIAL LOCAL SERVICES including fire protection, 911 response, schools, roads, hospitals and affordable housing. It doesn’t cut your taxes and lets just 33.4% of voters veto what nearly 67% want. Protect your vote and majority rule. Vote NO on Proposition 43.

***Vote Thresholds for Local Taxes.*** The State Constitution allows local governments to increase taxes with local voter approval.

Increases in some types of local taxes require a two-thirds vote to approve them, while other types of taxes require a majority (more than half) vote to approve them.
Some local tax increases are approved permanently, while others are approved for a limited period of time.
Before those taxes expire, voters can be asked whether to extend them.

This would generally be popular with anti-tax sentiment but opposed by fire, teachers, etc. The title says "LIMITS VOTERS' ABILITY TO RAISE REVENUES FOR LOCAL GOVERNMENT SERVICES" — a negative-sounding title from the AG (Bonta is a Democrat, and the Legislature placed this on the ballot). Actually the AG's title is quite negative, which would hurt the Yes campaign.

Also note it's a legislative constitutional amendment placed by the Legislature (which is Democratic-controlled, and the Legislature voted to place it). Wait, ACA 22 by Wicks — Democrats put it on the ballot to counter Howard Jarvis. The legislature passed it. So the Democratic legislature is against it, and it appears on the ballot as a measure backed by tax groups.

Hmm, so the "Yes" side is the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association; the "No" side is firefighters, teachers, nurses, and the Democratic establishment. Actually, there's a relevant precedent: In 1978 Prop 13 passed with 65%. Tax-limitation measures tend to do well in California. But recently, the AG's title here is quite negative.

Let me research polls for Prop 43 2026. Also check what happened in 2024 — there was a similar measure? Actually in 2024, ACA 1 (Ward) lowered the vote threshold for local affordable housing bonds from two-thirds to 55% — it was Prop 5 in November 2024, and it was defeated 38-62%. That's the opposite direction: voters rejected lowering the threshold. That suggests voters lean toward higher thresholds / taxpayer protection. Hmm, but Prop 5's defeat was largely attributed to a strong opposition campaign (No on 5 raised a lot, including from anti-YIMBY groups and also from those concerned about... ). Actually No on Prop 5 raised ~$7M vs Yes ~$10M. Prop 5 failed badly.

Now Prop 43 is essentially "close the loophole" created by the California Supreme Court's decision in California Cannabis Coalition v. City of San Diego (2017), which held that voter-initiated special taxes need only a majority vote.

### Summary
Placed on the ballot via 2025-2026 Assembly Constitutional Amendment 22 (ACA 22), Proposition 43 proposes adding Section 4.5 to Article XII of the California Constitution.
The measure increases the approval threshold for citizen-initiated local special tax measures, requiring a two-thirds (66.67%) vote to enact, extend, or raise special taxes at the local level.

Proposition 43 is forecast as a higher bars to pass measure whose Yes vote leans Republican . How this is built
Proposition 43 is forecast as a higher bars to pass measure whose Yes vote leans Republican . Comparable measures from 2018 to 2024 set how far its Yes share moves with California 's partisanship, and each county moves with its own age, education, race and density mix as well as its 2024 presidential vote, so no two counties share a margin by default. How it reached the ballot moves it further. Polls then pull the forecast toward them by recency and size, after splitting undecided voters two to one for No. Sources: elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/ccrov/2026/june/26179jj.pdf), growsf.org (https://growsf.org/news/2026-07-02-14-state-measures/), ppic.org (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), escholarship.org (https://escholarship.org/content/qt3w14s99c/qt3w14s99c.pdf). ## Proposition 43: Limits Voters' Ability to Raise Revenues for Local Government Services. Legislative Constitutional Amendment.
### Summary
Placed on the ballot via 2025-2026 Assembly Constitutional Amendment 22 (ACA 22), Proposition 43 proposes adding Section 4.5 to Article XII of the California Constitution.
The measure increases the approval threshold for citizen-initiated local special tax measures, requiring a two-thirds (66.67%) vote to enact, extend, or raise special taxes at the local level.

PROP
43
LIMITS VOTERS’ ABILITY TO RAISE REVENUES FOR LOCAL GOVERNMENT SERVICES. LEGISLATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by the Legislature
Limits voters’ ability to pass voter-proposed local special taxes by increasing percentage of votes needed to approve such ballot measures from a majority (over 50%) to two-thirds, beginning January 1, 2027. Fiscal Impact: Possibility that local government tax revenues will not go up as much in the future due to a higher vote threshold for certain taxes. Supporters: California Taxpayers Association; Family Business Association of California; California Hispanic Chambers of Commerce Opponents: California Professional Firefighters; California Federation of Teachers; Nurse Alliance of SEIU CA.
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: Certain local government taxes would require two-thirds approval by voters.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: Certain local government taxes could continue to be approved by voters with a majority vote.
ARGUMENTS
PRO
Prop. 43 protects taxpayers by restoring Proposition 13’s two-thirds vote requirement to pass local special taxes, including sales taxes, real estate taxes and utility taxes. Courts have allowed special interests to pass earmarked tax increases with fewer votes. Prop. 43 closes this loophole, protecting taxpayers, homeowners and renters. Vote yes.
CON
PROPOSITION 43 LIMITS VOTERS’ ABILITY TO FUND ESSENTIAL LOCAL SERVICES including fire protection, 911 response, schools, roads, hospitals and affordable housing. It doesn’t cut your taxes and lets just 33.4% of voters veto what nearly 67% want. Protect your vote and majority rule. Vote NO on Proposition 43.

# Proposition 43
Limits Voters’ Ability to Raise Revenues for Local Government Services.
Legislative Constitutional Amendment.
## Analysis of Measure
### Background
***Vote Thresholds for Local Taxes.*** The State Constitution allows local governments to increase taxes with local voter approval.
Tax increases can be put on a ballot by voters or a local governing board (such as a city council or board of supervisors).
Increases in some types of local taxes require a two-thirds vote to approve them, while other types of taxes require a majority (more than half) vote to approve them.
Some local tax increases are approved permanently, while others are approved for a limited period of time.
Before those taxes expire, voters can be asked whether to extend them.
### Proposal
***Requires Certain Local Taxes Receive Two-Thirds Approval by Voters.*** Under current law, local taxes that are used for a specific purpose require a two-thirds vote to be approved.
These are called special taxes.
However, recent court decisions have allowed special taxes that are *proposed by voters* to be approved with a majority vote.
Under Proposition 43, beginning on January 1, 2027, any new, increased, or extended local special taxes proposed by voters would require a two-thirds vote.

Very clear. All polls show the "No" side ahead by 10-13 points. The forecast gives No a 97% chance. Also the negative ballot title, the broad coalition opposing (local government associations, labor, housing advocates), and the fact that even the measure's author (Assemblymember Wicks) opposes it.

So the answer: the "No" side is more likely to win. Given the question "Which side is more likely to win? Answer with only yes or no" — presumably asking whether the "Yes" side is more likely to win. Answer: no.

Hmm, but ambiguity: "Which side is more likely to win?" answer with only yes or no — that's odd phrasing. The likely intent: "Is the yes side more likely to win?" So answer "no".

Actually, it could be interpreted as: the two sides are "yes" and "no", and we should pick which one. Either way, the answer is "no" — the No side wins.

Great, both interpretations converge to "no".
